newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan officials talk; blasts kill five.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan officials talk; blasts kill five.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani officials ended a second day of talks on Saturday but declined comment on whether they had narrowed their differences over the volatile Himalayan territory of Kashmir.

The talks coincided with two explosions at the central bus station in Jammu, the winter capital of India's Jammu and Kashmir state, in which at least five people were killed and several wounded, the United News of India (UNI) news agency said. There was no immediate word on who was behind the blasts.
In Srinagar, the state's summer capital, police said they fired warning shots in the air to disperse a small group of Kashmiri separatists, protesting at the India-Pakistan talks.
Pakistan's foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad and his Indian opposite number Salman Haidar made only brief comments after their three rounds of talks, including one over lunch.
"I shall rapidly withdraw from the realm of forecasting," Haidar told reporters when asked if he expected a breakthrough.
Asked if he was optimistic about the outcome, Ahmad said: "We diplomats are always hopeful."
Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesman, Khalid Saleem, said the delegations would meet for a third day on Sunday.
"All substantive issues came in for further discussion," he said. "Kashmir is an integral part of the discussions."
Earlier on Saturday Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda briefly met negotiators from both sides at his residence.
The two sides have pledged to make no public comment until their discussions, due to end on Monday, are over.
But the Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency said Ahmad had told Deve Gowda Pakistan would not put the thorny Kashmir dispute on hold while the two countries tackle other problems.
"There has to be some meaningful progress on the core issue of Kashmir before we address other matters," PTI quoted Ahmad as telling Deve Gowda. His reported remarks could not be confirmed.
PTI said the Indian delegation had stressed New Delhi's refusal to consider anything that would disturb India's secular unity and jeopardise its sovereignty (over Kashmir).

The talks are the first since January, 1994, when a dialogue foundered on Kashmir. Tension over the disputed Himalayan region sparked two of the three wars the two countries, now threshold nuclear powers, have fought since independence in 1947.
India accuses Pakistan of arming Moslem rebels fighting in the two thirds of Kashmir under Indian control.
Pakistan, which holds the rest of Kashmir, denies the charge, but says it supports the Kashmiris politicallly.
Mirwaiz Omar Farooq, leader of Kashmir's All Parties Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, criticised India and Pakistan for keeping Kashmiris out of any discussions on their future.
"We don't see this as a bilateral issue," he told Reuters by telephone. "It's not a territorial or regional dispute they can discuss by themselves...The Kashmiris must be involved."
Farooq was among a dozen Hurriyat leaders held for five hours in Delhi on Friday to block a protest against the talks.
The governor of Jammu and Kashmir, K.V. Krishna Rao, said Pakistan should show its sincerity by reining in the guerrillas.

"Pakistan should stop infiltrating militants into Kashmir and hand over the Kashmiri youths undergoing training in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir to India to give peace a chance to flourish," PTI quoted him as telling 200 former militants who have joined the paramilitary border security force.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir since the start of an armed revolt there in January 1990.
Hindu migrants from Kashmir staged noisy protests in New Delhi on Saturday against last week's killings of seven members of their community by unidentified gunmen, witnesses said.

Twelve Hindu families left their homes in the Moslem-dominated Kashmir Valley on Friday and arrived in Jammu, where they told reporters they feared for their lives after the killings in Sangrampur, a village in Budgam district.
